Verdict: the fault is host-local — web-07 — not the release and not the database. The split by host is unambiguous: the three healthy hosts average around 118 ms while web-07 averages roughly 940 ms, about 8.0x the fleet baseline, and every one of the sample's requests over 500 ms sits on web-07. If the new build were slow, all four hosts would be slow together, because they run identical code behind the same balancer; if the database were the bottleneck, latency would rise on every host at once, since they share it. A single-host signature points below the application: here it is a failing SSD pushing its writes into retry, so every request the load balancer sent to web-07 waited on storage. The proof is the counterfactual already in the data — the same endpoint, same hour, same build is fast on three hosts. Fix: cordon web-07 at the balancer and replace the drive; nothing in the application changed. Keep the per-host latency split as a standing panel; it settles this argument in one glance next time.

Verdict: one host, ord-09. Its average latency is roughly 860 ms against a fleet baseline near 97 ms — a 8.9x gap — and the query for requests over 500 ms returns only ord-09; the other three hosts have none. That distribution acquits yesterday's deploy: code faults do not respect host boundaries behind a load balancer, but this fault does, perfectly. It also acquits shared dependencies, which would tax all hosts equally. The mechanism on ord-09 is ord-09's network interface dropping to a renegotiated 100 Mb/s link after a switch flap, so large order payloads crawled. 'Only some users affected' is exactly what a single bad host behind a balancer looks like — roughly one request in four lands on it. Fix: reseat or replace the cable/NIC on ord-09 and confirm the link negotiates at full speed; the application never changed. Until then, draining ord-09 restores the fleet, because the remaining hosts are demonstrably healthy at baseline.

Error alerts fired for cart-api an hour into the v2.15.0 canary (25% of traffic). The on-call wants to know whether to roll back or look at the database first. Events are in error_events(ts, version, endpoint, status). Decide from the evidence.
A canary question is answered by comparing versions on the same endpoint in the same window — if the errors follow the version, the database is a bystander.

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: {"status": "ok"}

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: 80 row(s) affected

arguments.sql: SELECT version, COUNT(*) AS total, SUM(CASE WHEN status >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS errors FROM error_events GROUP BY version

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
version | total | errors
v2.14.0 | 40 | 1
v2.15.0 | 40 | 24

Verdict: roll back the canary — the errors belong to v2.15.0. In the same window on the same endpoint, v2.15.0 failed 24 of 40 requests (60.0%) while v2.14.0 failed 1 of 40 (2.5%, background noise). Both versions hit the same database, the same network, and the same downstream services, so a shared-dependency theory cannot explain a split this clean. The mechanism is v2.15.0 serializing the checkout payload with a field the payment client rejects, so its calls fail validation downstream. This is what the canary is for: at 25% the blast radius is contained, and the old version's clean line proves the system around the deploy is healthy. Fix: roll back the canary to 0% and fix the payload contract; the error is version-shaped, not load-shaped. Do not spend the incident on the database — its only symptom here is being downstream of a bad build.

Error rate for the recommendations service, by hour: 06:00 0.2%, 07:00 0.3%, 08:00 0.2%, 09:00 11.8%, 10:00 12.4%, 11:00 11.9%. Deploys today: recommendations v9.1 at 08:57; all other services deployed yesterday or earlier. Traffic volume is flat all morning. Give me a structured diagnosis: evidence, reading, verdict.

Structured diagnosis:

| Evidence | Reading |
|---|---|
| Error rate flat at 0.2–0.3% for three hours | The system was healthy on the old build under the same load |
| Rate steps to ~12% at 09:00 and holds | A step, not a ramp: something switched at a moment in time |
| v9.1 deployed at 08:57, the only deploy that day | The step and the deploy share a timestamp to the minute |
| Traffic volume flat | Load did not change, so load explains nothing |
| No other service deployed | The change surface is exactly one artifact |

Verdict: v9.1 is the fault, with the strongest evidence class incident work has — a step change coincident with a single change, on a flat background. Ramps implicate capacity and growth; steps implicate events, and the only event at 09:00 is the deploy. A 12% plateau (rather than 100%) fits a defect on a subset of requests — a payload variant, a locale, a code path — which is also why pre-production tests passed. Action: roll back v9.1 and diff its behavior on the failing request class; do not let the flat traffic line seduce anyone into a capacity review. The deploy log is a diagnostic instrument: every incident timeline should be annotated with changes before the first graph is opened.

A Java service shows p99 latency spikes to 3 seconds every ~40 seconds, while p50 never moves. Its GC log shows full collections pausing 2.8s, also every ~40 seconds, and heap occupancy sawtooths between 1.1 GB and 2.0 GB on a 2 GB heap. The team wants to add application instances. Structured diagnosis, please.

Structured diagnosis:

| Evidence | Reading |
|---|---|
| p99 spikes, p50 flat | Most requests are fast; a periodic event taxes a few |
| Spike period ≈ 40 s; full GC period ≈ 40 s | The periods match — same clock, same cause |
| Full GC pause 2.8 s; spike height ≈ 3 s | The magnitudes match too |
| Heap sawtooths 1.1→2.0 GB against a 2 GB ceiling | The heap fills completely, then pays a full collection |

Verdict: stop-the-world full GCs on an undersized (or over-retained) heap, not a capacity shortage. Two independent matches — period and magnitude — tie the latency spikes to the pauses: requests arriving during a 2.8 s pause wait ~2.8 s, which is precisely the p99 signature, while the p50 rides underneath untouched. Adding instances would multiply the number of JVMs doing this in unsynchronized misery and is the most expensive way to not fix it. The real questions are why the heap reaches its ceiling every 40 seconds (allocation rate versus live set) and why collection is full rather than young-gen. Fix the heap/live-set problem first; measure p99 after. Latency that ticks like a clock is a timer inside the process, and GC is the usual clock.

Clients report intermittent TLS errors: 'certificate has expired'. Retrying usually succeeds. Our cert was renewed last week and the main site checks out as valid for another 11 months. The errors cluster in one region. Structured diagnosis.

Structured diagnosis:

| Evidence | Reading |
|---|---|
| Error text: certificate expired | Some endpoint is presenting an actually expired cert |
| Retry usually succeeds | The client lands on a different endpoint that serves the new cert |
| Main site shows 11 months validity | The cert the checker reached is the renewed one |
| Errors cluster in one region | The stale cert lives on regional infrastructure |

Verdict: one load-balancer node (or a regional pool member) still serving the old, now-expired certificate. Intermittency plus retry-success is the fingerprint of a pool with mixed members: each connection draws a node, most hold the renewed cert, one holds the corpse. The main-site check passing proves nothing about the pool — it samples whichever node answered, and it drew a healthy one. This is the general trap of verifying replicated systems by sampling once. Fix: enumerate every pool member in the region and check the presented certificate on each, by address, not by hostname; replace the stale cert and add per-member cert-expiry alerting. Any 'intermittent TLS' report after a renewal should be treated as a mixed-pool finding until a per-member sweep says otherwise.

An application server rejects requests with 'queue full' during peaks. Metrics: worker threads 200/200 busy, request queue depth hits its 500 cap, CPU at 45%, database latency normal, downstream calls normal. The team proposes raising the queue to 5000. Structured diagnosis.

Structured diagnosis:

| Evidence | Reading |
|---|---|
| Threads 200/200 busy, queue at cap | Every worker is occupied and work is piling up |
| CPU 45% | The workers are not computing — they are waiting |
| DB and downstream latency 'normal' on average | Averages hide the wait; something in the request path blocks |
| Rejections only at peaks | The block rate scales with concurrency, pointing at a shared contended resource |

Verdict: the workers are blocked on a contended resource — classically a lock, a small internal pool, or a synchronized section — not short of threads or queue. Busy threads plus idle CPU is the signature of waiting, and waiting threads plus a filling queue means the queue is a symptom. Raising it to 5000 would convert fast, honest rejections into 5000 requests timing out slowly, while adding memory pressure; it treats the thermometer. The hunt: thread dumps at peak, looking for the stack most workers share — that stack names the resource. Fix that contention (or its timeout) and the queue drains at the same thread count. Rule of the house: never enlarge a queue in front of blocked workers until a thread dump says what they are waiting for.

Incident log, in order: 14:02:11 db-primary: checkpoint write latency 4s. 14:02:19 app: request timeouts begin. 14:02:26 cache: eviction rate spikes. 14:02:40 queue: consumer lag grows. 14:03:05 lb: 502s start. Everyone is blaming the cache evictions. Who actually started this?

The cache did not start this; it is fourth in line. Read the log as a causal chain, not a popularity contest: the first anomaly is the database primary's checkpoint write latency at 14:02:11 — storage-level slowness on the primary. Eight seconds later, application requests begin timing out, which is what slow writes do to everything that commits. The cache eviction spike at 14:02:26 is a consequence wearing a costume: timed-out requests retry and re-read, working sets churn, and eviction follows the churn. Queue lag and load-balancer 502s are further echoes. Blaming the cache mistakes the loudest symptom for the first cause — evictions are visible and countable, checkpoint latency is one quiet line. The discipline: in any cascade, sort by timestamp and defend the earliest anomaly; everything after it needs a mechanism that connects it forward, and here every later event is explained by slow primary writes while nothing explains the checkpoint line except storage. Investigate the primary's disk or checkpoint configuration; the cache will calm down when the timeouts stop, untreated.

Our API returns waves of 429s at peak and the team is about to scale the fleet. The 429s come from our own rate limiter. Limiter config: 1000 requests/minute per API key. The biggest key belongs to our own web frontend's server-side renderer, which fans every page view out to ~30 API calls. Page views peak at 60/minute. Diagnose before we buy servers.

Do not buy servers; your frontend is rate-limiting itself. The arithmetic is already conclusive: 60 page views a minute times roughly 30 API calls per render is about 1,800 requests a minute from the renderer's single API key — nearly double the 1,000/minute per-key limit — so the limiter fires exactly at peak page traffic, which is why the 429 waves track the business's busiest minutes. The fleet behind the limiter is presumably idle-ish while this happens; scaling it adds capacity the limiter will never let the renderer reach. The design fault is treating a first-party, server-side caller as if it were an untrusted third party sharing a key with itself. Fixes, in order of preference: give the renderer its own key with a limit sized to its fan-out (or an internal trust tier), cache the renderer's repeated calls so a page view costs fewer API requests, and alert on limiter rejections by key so a first-party key topping the list is seen immediately. A 429 from your own limiter is a config diagnosis, never a capacity one.

Six identical workers process a file feed. Five are fine. Worker 4 skips every file whose name contains an underscore. Configs were 'copied from worker 3'. The workers' filter is driven by a filename pattern in an environment setting. Where do you look first, and why are you confident?

At worker 4's copy of the pattern setting — specifically at what the copy actually contains, not what it was supposed to contain. The confidence comes from the shape of the failure: it is one worker out of six running the same code on the same feed, and its failure is not random or load-shaped but semantic — it rejects a well-defined class of filenames. Code defects do not single out a worker; data and configuration do, and a pattern-based skip that discriminates on underscores is a filter behaving exactly as configured. 'Copied from worker 3' is the tell rather than the reassurance: copies drift through shell escaping, and an underscore-adjacent pattern is precisely the kind that gets mangled — an escaped character class, a doubled backslash, a glob pasted where a regex was expected. Diff worker 4's effective environment against worker 3's byte for byte; the difference will be small, typographic, and entirely sufficient. General rule: when one replica misbehaves semantically, diff its inputs — config, environment, data — before reading shared code, because the code has five alibis.

Two availability zones. Services in AZ-a report AZ-b services 'down' (connection timeouts). Services in AZ-b report the same about AZ-a. Health checks run inside each zone pass for local services. Users in both zones are affected. Both zones' hosts are up. What is the fault domain?

The fault domain is the network between the zones — an inter-AZ partition — and the evidence is the symmetry. Each zone sees the other as down while its own services pass local health checks; if AZ-b's services had actually failed, AZ-b's local checks would fail and AZ-a's view would be accurate but one-sided. Instead both sides report the identical, mirrored symptom, which is what a severed link looks like from inside either half: every cross-zone call times out, every intra-zone call succeeds, and both halves honestly conclude the other is dead. Hosts being 'up' is consistent — they are up, to themselves. The user impact in both zones follows because real request paths cross zones (replicas, queues, auth), so a partition taxes everyone. Action: treat it as a network incident — check inter-AZ links, routing, and any change to cross-zone security groups or peering in the last hours — and shed cross-zone dependencies gracefully where possible. Do not restart services on either side: restarting healthy services into a partition only adds recovery load when the link heals. Mirrored 'the other side is down' reports are a partition until proven otherwise.

Capstone. A payments platform is slow and erroring. Signals: (1) latency is high only on hosts pay-01 and pay-02 of six; (2) those two hosts were rebuilt yesterday; (3) error rate is elevated on all six hosts equally; (4) the shared connection pool shows saturation at peak; (5) a config release went out this morning fleet-wide. Untangle: how many distinct faults are there, and which signals belong to which?

There are two distinct faults here, and the incident goes wrong the moment anyone insists on one. Fault one is host-local and explains signals 1 and 2: latency concentrated on pay-01 and pay-02, the two hosts rebuilt yesterday. Fleet-wide causes do not respect host boundaries; rebuilds do. Something in the rebuild — an image difference, a missing tuning parameter, a driver or kernel setting — made those two hosts slow, and the correct move is a configuration diff of a rebuilt host against a healthy one, not a fleet action. Fault two is fleet-wide and explains signals 3 and 5: errors elevated equally on all six hosts, beginning with a fleet-wide config release this morning. Equal distribution across healthy and rebuilt hosts alike is the signature of a shared change, and the release is the only fleet-wide event on the board. Signal 4, pool saturation at peak, belongs to neither as a root cause: it is the arithmetic consequence of both — slow hosts hold connections longer and erroring requests retry into the pool — which is why 'fix the pool' would have treated the shadow of two faults and cured neither. The method that untangles this: partition the signals by their distribution (host-local versus fleet-wide) before assigning causes. Every signal's shape tells you the size of its fault's blast radius, and causes must match the shapes of their effects. Chase the rebuild diff and the config release in parallel, with two owners, and let the pool recover on its own.
